summary: Follow-up part for the layer DT.4 (effective applications). It decomposes the proofs that the first pass left as route paragraphs: Baker's theorem on superelliptic and hyperelliptic equations and the Schinzel–Tijdeman theorem, in the explicit form of Bérczes–Evertse–Győry (2013) over the S-integers of a number field, and Tijdeman's effective finiteness theorem for Catalan's equation. The superelliptic proof is planned on two tracks: an effective track that rests only on the unit-equation theorems already planned in DT.4 (Győry's theorem for finitely generated groups), Siegel's identity and the class-group, S-unit and Minkowski facts planned here, and the explicit track of BEG, which adds discriminant estimates for the auxiliary fields (BEG §3.1, §4), class number and regulator bounds, small representatives modulo powers of S-units, Baker-type bounds at an arbitrary place, and the explicit Thue and Pell bounds of Győry–Yu. It also supplies the interfaces the first review asked to split: S-unit rank and the kernel and lattice of the S-logarithmic map, principal generators of class-group powers, the extension of Yu's p-adic bound to an arbitrary number field (including one logarithm), and the superelliptic ideal-power and height estimates; and it answers ArithmeticStatistics' request for a uniform bound on the number of solutions of cubic Thue equations. BEG's estimate (5.19) omits a class-number factor and (5.12) loses n; the independent review repairs both, the infinite-place normalization and the nonvanishing argument, and recomputes the final absorption. The exact Győry–Yu inputs are now identified, including the Loher–Masser height-product theorem; the corrected constant of their Theorem 2.3 is recorded and propagated to the ℤ-case statement.

nodes.title: Linear forms in logarithms of positive rationals with separated heights
nodes.statement: Let n ≥ 1, let a_1, …, a_n be positive rational numbers different from 1, let b ∈ ℤ^n and put Λ := b_1 log a_1 + ⋯ + b_n log a_n (real logarithms). For a positive rational a = u/w in lowest terms put H(a) := max(u, w) and A_j := max(log H(a_j), 0.16). If Λ ≠ 0 and B ≥ max_j |b_j|, then log|Λ| > −C(n)·A_1⋯A_n·log(eB) with C(n) := (en/2)·30^{n+3}·n^{3.5}. In particular, if H(a_j) ≤ A′ for j < n and H(a_n) ≤ A with A, A′ ≥ 2, then |Λ| > exp(−C(n)·(log A′)^{n−1}·log A·log(eB)). This is stronger than the two Baker-type inputs of Tijdeman's Catalan paper (his Theorem 2, exponent 2n² + 16n on log A′, and Baker's Theorem B, with Q* log Q* in place of Q*), so both are replaced by it.
proofSteps: Apply DT.3/matveev-corollary-linear-form-bound with K = ℚ (degree D = 1, real, so κ = 1), α_j = a_j and λ_j = log a_j, which is a nonzero logarithm of a_j because a_j ≠ 1.

The absolute logarithmic height of a positive rational a = u/w in lowest terms is log max(u, w) (Rat.mulHeight₁_eq_max), and |log a| = |log u − log w| ≤ log max(u, w); hence A_j ≥ max(D·h(a_j), |λ_j|, 0.16).
Matveev's constant is C_1(n, 1)·D²·log(eD) with C_1(n, 1) ≤ (en/2)·30^{n+3}·n^{3.5} and D²·log(eD) = 1; the factor log(eB*) with B* = max|b_j| is at most log(eB).
For the second form bound A_j ≤ log A′ for j < n and A_n ≤ log A, which holds because A, A′ ≥ 2 > e^{0.16}.
acceptance: For n = 1 the bound is |b_1 log a_1| > exp(−C(1)·A_1·log(eB)), consistent with the trivial bound |log a_1| ≥ log(1 + 1/H(a_1)).
The hypothesis a_j ≠ 1 is needed: Matveev's corollary takes nonzero logarithms.
With a_1 = 2, a_2 = 3, b = (b_1, b_2) and B = max(|b_1|, |b_2|) it gives |b_1 log 2 + b_2 log 3| > exp(−C(2)·log 3·log 2·log(eB)), the shape used for |2^{b_1}3^{b_2} − 1|.

nodes.title: Catalan's equation reduces to distinct prime exponents
nodes.statement: Let x, y, m, n be integers ≥ 2 with x^m − y^n = 1. For every prime p dividing m and every prime q dividing n, the integers X := x^{m/p} and Y := y^{n/q} are ≥ 2 and satisfy X^p − Y^q = 1, with X^p = x^m and Y^q = y^n; moreover p ≠ q. Consequently an upper bound for X^p and Y^q over all solutions with distinct prime exponents bounds x^m and y^n, and then m, n ≤ log(x^m)/log 2 and log(y^n)/log 2.
hypotheses: x, y, m, n ∈ ℤ with x, y, m, n ≥ 2
p, q primes with p ∣ m and q ∣ n
proofSteps: Every integer ≥ 2 has a prime divisor (Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd), so p and q exist; X^p = x^m and Y^q = y^n by the power-of-a-power rule, and X, Y ≥ 2 because x, y ≥ 2 and m/p, n/q ≥ 1.
If p = q then X^p = Y^p + 1 > Y^p forces X ≥ Y + 1, hence X^p − Y^p ≥ (Y + 1)^p − Y^p ≥ p·Y^{p−1} ≥ 4, contradicting X^p − Y^p = 1.
Since x ≥ 2, m ≤ log(x^m)/log 2, and likewise for n.
acceptance: For 3² − 2³ = 1 the lemma gives (X, Y, p, q) = (3, 2, 2, 3).
For x^4 − y^n = 1 with p = 2 one obtains X = x², so solutions with composite exponents are not lost.
The conclusion p ≠ q fails for the equation X^p − Y^p = 0, which is why the right-hand side 1 matters.

nodes.title: Catalan's equation when one exponent is 2
nodes.statement: There is an effectively computable absolute constant C_2 such that for all primes p ≠ q with 2 ∈ {p, q} and all integers X, Y ≥ 2 with X^p − Y^q = 1 one has p, q, X, Y ≤ C_2. Explicitly: if q = 2 then X^p = Y² + 1 and p ≤ 40^{92} by the Schinzel–Tijdeman theorem for f = T² + 1, b = 1 (corrected constant of beg-schinzel-tijdeman-bound; BEG's printed constant would give 40^{80}); if p = 2 then Y^q = X² − 1 and q ≤ 40^{92} by the same theorem for f = T² − 1, b = 1; for each such exponent ≥ 3 Baker's superelliptic theorem bounds X and Y.
hypotheses: p, q primes, p ≠ q, 2 ∈ {p, q}
proofSteps: Case q = 2: X^p = f(Y) with f := T² + 1 ∈ ℤ[T] of degree N = 2, without multiple zeros, and b = 1. Since X ∉ {0, ±1}, beg-schinzel-tijdeman-bound with K = ℚ, S = ∅ (the effective content is DT.4/schinzel-tijdeman-theorem; its unknowns renamed: its y is X, its x is Y and its exponent is p) gives p ≤ (10N²)^{46N}·e^{15Nĥ} = 40^{92}, because ĥ = log max(1, |b|, |coefficients|) = 0.

For each prime p with 3 ≤ p ≤ 40^{92} the equation X^p = Y² + 1 is a superelliptic equation b·X^p = f(Y) with exponent p ≥ 3 and deg f = 2 ≥ 2, so DT.4/baker-superelliptic-theorem bounds log max(1, |X|), log max(1, |Y|) by (12)^{14p³·8}, an explicit function of p. (p = 2 is excluded because p ≠ q.)
Case p = 2: Y^q = X² − 1 = f(X) with f := T² − 1, which has the two simple zeros ±1; Y ∉ {0, ±1}, so again q ≤ 40^{92}, and for each prime q ≥ 3 below this bound Baker's theorem bounds X and Y.

Take C_2 as the maximum of the finitely many bounds so obtained. This replaces Tijdeman's appeal to Lebesgue's theorem (no solution of X^p = Y² + 1 with Y ≥ 1) by an effective bound, which suffices for an effective finiteness statement.
acceptance: The bound 40^{92} is (10·2²)^{46·2}, the value of the corrected BEG bound at N = 2, s = 1, d = 1, D_K = 1, P_S = 1, ĥ = 0.
The solution 3² − 2³ = 1 has p = 2 and is covered by this node, with q = 3 ≤ 40^{92}.
Without the restriction Y ≥ 2 the equation X^p = Y² + 1 has the solution (X, Y) = (1, 0) for every p, which is why the Schinzel–Tijdeman hypothesis X ∉ {0, ±1} is checked.

nodes.title: The factorisations x − 1 = p^{δ₁}ρ^q and y + 1 = q^{δ₂}σ^p
nodes.statement: Let p, q be distinct odd primes and x, y ≥ 2 integers with x^p − y^q = 1. Then there are δ₁, δ₂ ∈ {−1, 0} and integers ρ, σ ≥ 2 with x − 1 = p^{δ₁}ρ^q and y + 1 = q^{δ₂}σ^p; moreover δ₁ = −1 exactly when p ∣ x − 1, and δ₂ = −1 exactly when q ∣ y + 1, in which case p ∣ ρ, respectively q ∣ σ. Substituting gives (p^{δ₁}ρ^q + 1)^p − (q^{δ₂}σ^p − 1)^q = 1. (Tijdeman allows δ₁, δ₂ ∈ {−1, 0, 1}, which also covers p = 2; for odd primes the value 1 does not occur.)
proofSteps: Write y^q = x^p − 1 = (x − 1)·Φ with Φ := 1 + x + ⋯ + x^{p−1}. Any common divisor of x − 1 and Φ divides Φ(1) = p, so gcd(x − 1, Φ) ∈ {1, p}.
If p ∤ x − 1 the two factors are coprime positive integers whose product is a q-th power, so x − 1 = ρ^q (δ₁ = 0).

If p ∣ x − 1, lifting the exponent (DT.3/p-adic-valuation-of-power-minus-one with a = x − 1, b = p) gives v_p(x^p − 1) = v_p(x − 1) + 1, so v_p(Φ) = 1; every other prime divides at most one factor. Hence v_p(x − 1) = q·v_p(y) − 1 and v_ℓ(x − 1) ≡ 0 (mod q) for ℓ ≠ p, i.e. p·(x − 1) is a q-th power ρ^q with p ∣ ρ (δ₁ = −1, ρ ≥ p ≥ 3).

Symmetrically x^p = y^q + 1 = (y + 1)·Ψ with Ψ := y^{q−1} − y^{q−2} + ⋯ + 1 (q odd), gcd(y + 1, Ψ) ∣ Ψ(−1) = q, and lifting the exponent for (−y)^q − 1 with a = −(y + 1) gives δ₂ ∈ {−1, 0}; y + 1 ≥ 3 forces σ ≥ 2.

ρ ≥ 2: ρ = 1 would force δ₁ = 0 and x = 2, so y^q + 1 = 2^p; but Ψ is a sum of q odd terms, hence odd, and Ψ > 1 for y ≥ 2, so (y + 1)·Ψ is not a power of 2. σ ≥ 2: σ = 1 would give y + 1 ∈ {1, 1/q}. Hence Tijdeman's case (a) ('ρ = 1 or σ = 1') does not occur when p and q are both odd.
acceptance: For the excluded even case 3² − 2³ = 1 one has x − 1 = 2 = 2^{1}·1^3, which needs δ₁ = 1: the restriction to odd primes is essential for δ ∈ {−1, 0}.
If p ∣ x − 1 then p·(x − 1) is a perfect q-th power (δ₁ = −1).
The identity (p^{δ₁}ρ^q + 1)^p − (q^{δ₂}σ^p − 1)^q = 1 holds by substitution.

nodes.title: The smaller exponent is polylogarithmic in the larger
nodes.statement: There are effectively computable absolute constants c₁, c₂ > 0 such that for all distinct odd primes p, q and integers x, y ≥ 2 with x^p − y^q = 1: if p > q then q ≤ c₁(log p)^{c₂}, and if q > p then p ≤ c₁(log q)^{c₂}. With the logarithmic-form bound of this layer one may take c₂ = 3.
hypotheses: x, y ≥ 2 integers with x^p − y^q = 1
proofSteps: Use cassels-type-factorisations; for odd p, q it gives ρ, σ ≥ 2, so Tijdeman's case (a) (ρ = 1 or σ = 1) is empty and only his case (b) remains.

Case p > q: from (x − 1)^p < y^q + 1 < (y + 1)^q and the identity of the previous node, with |log(1 + a)| ≤ a (a > 0) and |log((1 − a)^q + a^q)| ≤ 2aq for 0 ≤ a ≤ 1/2, one gets 0 < |δ₁ p log p − δ₂ q log q + pq log(ρ/σ)| ≤ p/(p^{δ₁}ρ^q) + 2q/(q^{δ₂}σ^p) ≤ 3p²/ρ^q, using that p > q forces y > x and hence q^{δ₂}σ^p > p^{δ₁}ρ^q. The form is nonzero because it is the logarithm of (x − 1)^p/(y + 1)^q < 1.

If q ≤ 10 log p there is nothing to prove. Otherwise ρ ≥ 2 gives ρ^{q/2} > p^{5 log 2} > 3p², so the form is < exp(−(q/2) log ρ) (Tijdeman (17)); this forces |log(ρ/σ)| ≤ 2 log p/q + 1 < 2 (Tijdeman (18)), hence σ < e²ρ < ρ⁴ and H(ρ/σ) ≤ ρ⁴.

separated-height-logarithmic-form-bound with n ≤ 3, the rationals p, q, ρ/σ (dropping terms with zero coefficient), B = p² and A_1, A_2 ≤ log p, A_3 ≤ 4 log ρ gives a lower bound exp(−C·(log p)³·log ρ); comparing exponents yields q < c₁(log p)³.

The case q > p is the mirror image: x > y gives p^{δ₁}ρ^q ≥ q^{δ₂}σ^p − 1, the upper bound becomes ≤ 4q²/σ^p, and the same lower bound with the roles of (p, ρ) and (q, σ) exchanged gives p < c₁(log q)³. Tijdeman states only that this case is similar (sourceIssues).

Before using Matveev, remove every zero logarithm and every zero coefficient. The positive rational arguments then have chosen nonzero real logarithms. In the q > p case x > y gives x − 1 ≥ y ≥ (y + 1)/2; consequently the three-logarithm upper bound is at most 4q²/σ^p. Use A_i equal to the displayed admissible upper bounds, not merely bounded above by them.
acceptance: The bound is uniform: c₁, c₂ do not depend on x, y.
For odd p, q the equation 2^p − y^q = 1 has no solution (y^q + 1 = 2^p is impossible), so no separate case x = 2 is needed.
The nonvanishing of the three-logarithm form is proved from (x − 1)^p < (y + 1)^q, not assumed.

nodes.title: The larger exponent is bounded by an absolute constant
nodes.statement: There is an effectively computable absolute constant C₁ such that for all distinct odd primes p, q and integers x, y ≥ 2 with x^p − y^q = 1 one has max(p, q) ≤ C₁.
hypotheses: x, y ≥ 2 integers with x^p − y^q = 1
proofSteps: For p > q use Tijdeman §5: a = (q^{δ₂}σ^p)⁻¹, β = (p^{δ₁}ρ^q + 1)/σ^q = x/σ^q. Then β^p q^{−δ₂q} = (1 − a)^q + a^q, so the logarithmic form is nonzero and negative. The small-exponent bound controls q by a power of log p; h(β) ≤ 2q log σ and |log β| ≤ 1 for large p. The separated-height bound on these two logarithms compared with the exponentially small upper bound controls p/log(p)^C.

For q > p carry out the following different normalization. Put a = (p^{δ₁}ρ^q)⁻¹ = 1/(x − 1) and β = (q^{δ₂}σ^p − 1)/ρ^p = y/ρ^p. The equation gives β^q p^{−δ₁p} = (1 + a)^p − a^p > 1. Hence 0 < q log β − δ₁p log p ≤ 2pa ≤ 2p²/ρ^q. For sufficiently large q, the small-exponent bound makes this at most exp(−(q/2) log ρ).

Also h(β) ≤ 2p log ρ and |log β| ≤ (p log p + 1)/q ≤ 1 for sufficiently large q. If δ₁ = 0, β > 1; if δ₁ = −1, q log β = −p log p + a positive exponentially small term, so β ≠ 1. Drop any zero coefficient and apply separated-height-logarithmic-form-bound to β and p. This yields a lower bound exp(−C(log q)^C′ log ρ), contradicting the upper bound when q is large.

All sufficiently-large thresholds are computable. The finitely many smaller exponent cases and the p > q case give one absolute computable upper bound; combine it with tijdeman-smaller-exponent-bound to bound both primes.
acceptance: The constant is absolute: it depends on neither x nor y.
The proof uses p ≥ 32 only to absorb 2q² into σ^{p/2}; smaller p are bounded trivially.
Together with the previous node both exponents are bounded.

nodes.title: Tijdeman's theorem on Catalan's equation
nodes.statement: There is an effectively computable constant C₀ such that every solution of x^m − y^n = 1 in integers x, y, m, n ≥ 2 satisfies m, n, x, y ≤ C₀ (Tijdeman's Theorem 1); in particular x^m, y^n ≤ C₀^{C₀}, which is the statement of DT.4/tijdeman-catalan-bound. (Mihăilescu proved that 3² − 2³ = 1 is the only solution; that proof is algebraic and is not planned in this layer.)
hypotheses: x, y, m, n ∈ ℤ, all ≥ 2
proofSteps: catalan-reduction-to-prime-exponents gives distinct primes p ∣ m, q ∣ n and X, Y ≥ 2 with X^p − Y^q = 1, X^p = x^m, Y^q = y^n.
If 2 ∈ {p, q}, catalan-exponent-two-cases bounds p, q, X, Y. Otherwise p, q are odd and tijdeman-larger-exponent-bound bounds max(p, q) by C₁.

For each of the finitely many pairs (p, q) of odd primes up to C₁, Y^q = X^p − 1 = f(X) with f := T^p − 1, which has p ≥ 3 simple zeros, and q ≥ 3; DT.4/baker-superelliptic-theorem bounds |X| and |Y|.
Hence X^p and Y^q are bounded, and then m ≤ log(x^m)/log 2, n ≤ log(y^n)/log 2 and x ≤ x^m, y ≤ y^n are bounded.
acceptance: The solution (x, y, m, n) = (3, 2, 2, 3) satisfies the bound for every admissible C₀ ≥ 3.
The theorem is effective: C₀ is assembled from the explicit constants of the logarithmic-form bound and of the superelliptic theorem.
It implies DT.4/tijdeman-catalan-bound, whose statement bounds only x^m and y^n.

nodes.title: Linear factors of a primitive irreducible binary form generate a fixed ideal
nodes.statement: Let F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] be an irreducible binary form of degree n ≥ 1 whose coefficients have greatest common divisor 1, with a₀ := F(1, 0) ≠ 0. Let θ be a zero of F(X, 1), L := ℚ(θ) (of degree n) and 𝔞_θ := the fractional ideal of 𝓞_L generated by 1 and θ. Then (i) the absolute norm of 𝔞_θ is 1/|a₀|; (ii) for (x, y) ∈ ℤ², x − θy ∈ 𝔞_θ and the integral ideal (x − θy)·𝔞_θ^{−1} has absolute norm |F(x, y)|; (iii) consequently, if F(x, y) = ±1 then (x − θy)𝓞_L = 𝔞_θ, so any two such solutions give elements x − θy differing by a unit of 𝓞_L.
hypotheses: F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] homogeneous of degree n ≥ 1, irreducible over ℚ, with coprime coefficients
θ a complex zero of F(X, 1), L = ℚ(θ)
proofSteps: Let G be the Galois closure of L and θ₁ = θ, …, θ_n the conjugates. In G[X], F(X, 1) = a₀∏_i(X − θ_i).

Gauss's lemma for content ideals over the Dedekind domain 𝓞_G (content-ideal-gauss-lemma) gives [F(X, 1)]_G = [a₀]_G·∏_i [1, θ_i]_G; since the coefficients of F are coprime integers the left side is 𝓞_G, so ∏_i [1, θ_i]_G = [a₀]_G^{−1}.
The absolute norm is invariant under the automorphisms of G and satisfies N_G(𝔞𝓞_G) = N_L(𝔞)^{[G:L]}; taking absolute norms gives N_L(𝔞_θ)^{n[G:L]} = |a₀|^{−n[G:L]}, hence (i).
x − θy lies in 𝔞_θ because x, y ∈ ℤ; the principal ideal (x − θy) has absolute norm |N_{L/ℚ}(x − θy)| = |∏_i(x − θ_i y)| = |F(x, y)|/|a₀|, and dividing by N_L(𝔞_θ) = 1/|a₀| gives (ii).
(iii): an integral ideal of norm 1 is the unit ideal.
acceptance: For F = X³ − 2Y³: a₀ = 1, θ = ∛2, 𝔞_θ = 𝓞_L, and x − θy is a unit exactly when F(x, y) = ±1.
For F = 2X² + XY + Y² (irreducible, primitive): N(𝔞_θ) = 1/2, so 𝔞_θ is not integral.
The primitivity hypothesis matters: for 2F the content is 2 and (i) fails.

nodes.title: A uniform bound for the number of solutions of Thue equations F(x, y) = 1
nodes.statement: For every n ≥ 3 there is an explicit N(n) such that for every binary form F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] of degree n with nonzero discriminant, #{(x, y) ∈ ℤ² : F(x, y) = 1} ≤ N(n); one may take N(n) := max(2·A(2, 2(n(n − 1)(n − 2) − 1)) + 2, 16), where A(2, r) = exp(12⁶(r + 1)) is the Evertse–Schlickewei–Schmidt bound for the number of solutions of a two-term unit equation in a group of rank r. In particular there is an absolute bound for cubic forms (N(3) ≤ 2·exp(12⁶·11) + 2). Sharper absolute values (12 by Delone–Nagell and Evertse, 10 by Bennett) are not planned here.
hypotheses: F ∈ ℤ[X, Y] homogeneous of degree n
proofSteps: If the coefficients of F have a common factor ≥ 2 there is no solution. Otherwise factor F = ∏_j G_j into irreducible primitive forms over ℤ (Gauss's lemma in ℤ[X, Y]); F(x, y) = 1 forces G_j(x, y) = ±1 for all j, and the G_j are pairwise non-proportional because disc F ≠ 0.

Some G_j of degree d ≥ 3: if G_j(1, 0) = 0 replace G_j by G_j(X, Y + kX) for some k with G_j(1, k) ≠ 0, a unimodular change of variables that preserves the number of solutions. Pick distinct zeros θ₁, θ₂, θ₃ of G_j(X, 1), M := ℚ(θ₁, θ₂, θ₃) (degree ≤ d(d − 1)(d − 2)) and one solution (x₀, y₀). By primitive-binary-form-linear-factor-ideal(iii) x − θ_i y = (x₀ − θ_i y₀)·ε_i with ε_i ∈ 𝓞_M^×.

Siegel's identity (DT.4/siegel-identity) turns this into a·(ε₁/ε₃) + b·(ε₂/ε₃) = 1 with fixed a, b ∈ M^×; every solution of a two-term unit equation is non-degenerate, so by DT.2/uniform-bound-nondegenerate-solutions applied to Γ = (𝓞_M^×)², of rank ≤ 2(n(n − 1)(n − 2) − 1) (Dirichlet), there are at most A(2, 2r) pairs.

Each pair determines λ = (x − θ₁y)/(x − θ₃y) and, for y ≠ 0, x/y = (θ₁ − λθ₃)/(1 − λ); a ratio determines the coprime solution up to the sign t = ±1 (t^d·G_j(x′, y′) = ±1); and y = 0 gives at most 2 solutions. Hence at most 2A + 2 solutions.

If all irreducible factors have degree at most two, select two distinct factors. Two linear equations G₁ = ±1, G₂ = ±1 give at most four points. A linear and an irreducible quadratic give at most two points on each of the four affine lines prescribed by the signs, hence at most eight: restriction of the quadratic cannot be constant, since its leading part would vanish on a rational direction and make the binary quadratic reducible. Two quadratics give, for each sign pair, the nonzero homogeneous quadratic ε₂G₁ − ε₁G₂ = 0, hence at most two lines through the origin and at most two points per line, giving sixteen. This handles mixed degrees without treating their difference as homogeneous.
acceptance: For n = 3 the bound is absolute, which is the request of ArithmeticStatistics:ST.1/fibres-of-the-embedding-are-uniformly-bounded.
F = X³ − 2Y³ has the solutions (1, 0) and (−1, −1) of F = 1, so N(3) ≥ 2 is forced.
The hypothesis disc F ≠ 0 is needed: F = (X − Y)³ has the infinitely many solutions (y + 1, y) of F = 1.

nodes.title: Voutier's lower bound for the height of an algebraic number
nodes.statement: Let α be a nonzero algebraic number of degree d that is not a root of unity. Then its absolute logarithmic height satisfies h(α) ≥ m(d), where m(1) := log 2 and m(d) := 2/(d·(log 3d)³) for d ≥ 2 (Voutier's Corollary 2; BEG Lemma 3.9).
hypotheses: α is not a root of unity
proofSteps: d = 1: α = u/w in lowest terms with α ≠ ±1, so max(|u|, |w|) ≥ 2 and h(α) = log max(|u|, |w|) ≥ log 2.

d ≥ 2: Voutier proves log M(α) > (1/4)(log log d/log d)³ for d ≥ 2 by the determinant method of Cantor and Straus (Fermat's little theorem gives a nonzero integer lower bound, Hadamard's inequality an upper bound); Corollary 2 combines this with Smyth's theorem for non-reciprocal α and with Boyd's computations for d ≤ 20, and d·h(α) = log M(α).
The case d ≥ 2 is not decomposed into nodes here (gap 'Voutier's height lower bound'); only the case d = 1 is used for equations over ℤ.

If α has degree e ≤ d, apply Voutier to e and use that e(log(3e))³ is increasing; degree-one elements have height at least log 2. Auxiliary root fields L_i generally have degree greater than one even when K = ℚ, so their units still require the higher-degree cutoff.
acceptance: For α = 2: h(2) = log 2 = m(1).
Roots of unity have height 0, so the hypothesis is necessary.

nodes.title: Yu's p-adic bound for algebraic numbers in an arbitrary number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d_K, 𝔓 a nonzero prime of 𝓞_K above the rational prime p, with ramification index e(𝔓) and residue degree f(𝔓), and |·|_𝔓 := N𝔓^{−ord_𝔓(·)} the normalised absolute value. Let n ≥ 1, α_1, …, α_n ∈ K^× and b ∈ ℤ^n with Λ := α_1^{b_1}⋯α_n^{b_n} − 1 ≠ 0. Put n′ := max(n, 2), let (α′_j) be (α_j) padded, when n = 1, by α′_2 := p with b_2 := 0, let K₀ := ℚ(α′_1, …, α′_{n′}) ⊆ K of degree d₀, 𝔭₀ := 𝔓 ∩ 𝓞_{K₀} and h_j ≥ max(h(α′_j), |log α′_j|/(10d₀), log p) (principal complex logarithm). Then ord_𝔓(Λ) = e(𝔓|𝔭₀)·ord_{𝔭₀}(Λ) < e(𝔓|𝔭₀)·Φ₀·log(d₀B) and hence log|Λ|_𝔓 > −e(𝔓|𝔭₀)·Φ₀·log(d₀B)·log N𝔓, where B := max(|b_1|, …, |b_n|, 3) and Φ₀ := 22000·(9.5(n′ + 1)d₀/√(log p))^{2(n′+1)}·(p^{f(𝔭₀)} − 1)·h_1⋯h_{n′}·log(10n′d₀h′), h′ := max(h_j, 1). In particular |Λ|_𝔓 ≥ (e·max(1, max|b_j|))^{−C} with C depending only on d_K, n, p, N𝔓 and the h_j, which is the p-adic hypothesis of DT.4/gyory-equation-exponent-bound.
hypotheses: K a number field, 𝔓 ∣ p a nonzero prime of 𝓞_K
proofSteps: Padding: for n = 1 adjoin α′_2 := p with exponent 0; Λ is unchanged, ℚ(α_1, p) = ℚ(α_1), h(p) = log p and |log p|/(10d₀) ≤ log p, so the admissible h_2 = log p does not depend on α_1.
Apply DT.3/yu-explicit-p-adic-bound to (α′_j), b and the prime 𝔭₀ of the generated field K₀ (its hypothesis K = ℚ(α) is met by K₀); the condition b ≠ 0 holds because Λ ≠ 0 forces some b_j ≠ 0.
Restriction: Λ ∈ K₀, and for x ∈ K₀^× one has ord_𝔓(x) = e(𝔓|𝔭₀)·ord_{𝔭₀}(x) (multiplicativity of ramification in towers); the residue degree in the bound is that of 𝔭₀ over p.
Conversion: log|Λ|_𝔓 = −ord_𝔓(Λ)·log N𝔓; with e(𝔓|𝔭₀) ≤ [K : K₀] and log(d₀B) ≤ log d_K + log 3 + log(e·max(1, max|b_j|)) one reads off C.

For the field F generated by the logarithm arguments inside K, use valuation_liesOver for a prime of K above a prime of F: ord_𝔭(λ) = e(𝔭|𝔮) ord_𝔮(λ). Multiply by log N𝔭 for the normalized FinitePlace.mk absolute value. Yu 1994 permits arbitrary nonzero arguments, so padding a one-logarithm form by the rational prime with coefficient zero does not require that prime to be a local unit.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, n = 1, α_1 = 1 + p (p odd) and b_1 = b, the bound is consistent with the exact value ord_p((1 + p)^b − 1) = 1 + v_p(b) (DT.3/p-adic-valuation-of-power-minus-one).
If 𝔓 is unramified over 𝔭₀ the factor e(𝔓|𝔭₀) is 1 and the bound is Yu's bound read in K.
The padding by α′_2 = p never creates the excluded case α^b = 1, because b_2 = 0.

nodes.title: Baker-type lower bound for |α^b − 1|_v at an arbitrary place (BEG Proposition 3.10)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, n ≥ 2, α_1, …, α_n ∈ K^×, b ∈ ℤ^n not all zero, Λ := α_1^{b_1}⋯α_n^{b_n} − 1, Θ := ∏_i max(h(α_i), m(d)) with m(d) as in voutier-height-lower-bound, B := max(3, |b_1|, …, |b_n|), and for a place v of K put N(v) := 2 if v is infinite and N(v) := N𝔭 if v = 𝔭 is finite; |·|_v is normalised as in s-norm. If Λ ≠ 0 then log|Λ|_v > −c₁(n, d)·(N(v)/log N(v))·Θ·log B with c₁(n, d) := 12·(16ed)^{3n+2}·(log* d)², log* x := max(1, log x).
hypotheses: K a number field, d = [K : ℚ], n ≥ 2
proofSteps: At an infinite place of multiplicity a = 1 or 2 embed K into ℂ. Put Ξ = Σ b_i log α_i + 2b₀ log(−1), with |Im Ξ| ≤ π and |2b₀| ≤ 1 + nB. If |Λ| ≤ 1/2, Ξ is the principal logarithm of 1 + Λ, so 0 < |Ξ| ≤ 2|Λ|. If |Λ| > 1/2 the claimed lower bound is immediate. Remove zero logarithms and zero coefficients before applying DT.3/matveev-corollary-linear-form-bound.

Choose the genuinely admissible Matveev parameters A_i = d h(α_i) + π and A₀ = π. Thus Ω ≤ π F(d)^n Θ, where F(d) = d + π/m(d). The supplier gives a constant at most 2^{6(n+1)+20}, and log(eB′) ≤ (n+2)log B for B′ ≤ 1+nB. Consequently log |Λ|_v ≥ −2π·2^{6n+26}(n+2)d²log(ed) F(d)^n Θ log B − 2log 2.

For d = 1, F(d) ≤ 6. For d ≥ 2, F(d) ≤ 3d³: use m(d) = 2/(d(log(3d))³) and the decreasing function log(3d)³/d² for d ≥ 2. Also log(ed)/(log* d)² ≤ 2. Comparing with c₁(n,d)·2/log 2 at n = 2 bounds the main-coefficient ratio by 0.6 for d = 1 and 0.3 for d ≥ 2; successive n only decrease it. The remaining slack absorbs 2log 2 because Θ ≥ m(d)^n and log B ≥ log 3. This supplies the claimed constant without discarding d from the height parameters.

At a finite place the exact BEG constant uses Yu 2007, whose main theorem is a recorded gap. The Yu 1994 adapter provides an effective lower bound with a different constant; do not identify it with c₁(n,d). Normalize the valuation by log N𝔭 as in FinitePlace.mk.

nodes.title: The S-norm of an element of a number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field and S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K; the places of K in 'S' are S together with all infinite places. Normalise absolute values as in Bérczes–Evertse–Győry (2.1): |x|_v := |σ(x)| at a real place, |σ(x)|² at a complex place, and N𝔭^{−ord_𝔭(x)} at a finite place 𝔭 (in Mathlib: w(x)^{mult w} for w : InfinitePlace K, and the FinitePlace norm). The S-norm of x ∈ K is N_S(x) := ∏_{w infinite} w(x)^{mult w} · ∏_{𝔭 ∈ S} |x|_𝔭. For x ≠ 0 the product formula gives N_S(x) = ∏_{𝔭 ∉ S} |x|_𝔭^{−1}, the absolute norm of the part of the fractional ideal (x) supported outside S; for a fractional ideal of the S-integers generated by x_1, …, x_r, N_S([x_1, …, x_r]_S) := ∏_{𝔭 ∉ S} max_i |x_i|_𝔭^{−1}.

proofSteps: Definition. The two descriptions agree by the product formula (NumberField.prod_abs_eq_one) and the finite support of x ↦ |x|_𝔭 (FinitePlace.hasFiniteMulSupport).

nodes.title: The S-regulator of a number field
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, S a finite set of nonzero primes 𝔭_1, …, 𝔭_t of 𝓞_K, and s := t + #(infinite places). Let ε_1, …, ε_{s−1} be a fundamental system of S-units (a basis of 𝓞_S^× modulo torsion) and v_1, …, v_{s−1} any s − 1 of the s places in S ∪ S_∞. The S-regulator is R_S := |det(log|ε_i|_{v_j})_{i,j ≤ s−1}|, with the normalised absolute values of s-norm. It is independent of both choices; R_∅ = R_K (Mathlib's regulator), and R_S = h_S·R_K·∏_{i=1}^{t} log N𝔭_i, where h_S is the order of the subgroup of the class group generated by the classes of 𝔭_1, …, 𝔭_t. Consequently R_S ≤ h_K·R_K·(log P_S)^t with P_S := max_i N𝔭_i, and, using R_K ≥ 0.2, R_S ≥ R_K·∏_i log N𝔭_i ≥ 0.2·(log 2)^t.
hypotheses: S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K
a fundamental system of S-units (Tau Ceti Set.unit_fg_of_units gives finite generation)
proofSteps: Independence of the omitted place: the rows sum to zero by the product formula, so deleting any column changes the determinant only by sign.
Independence of the fundamental system: two systems differ by an element of GL_{s−1}(ℤ) modulo torsion, and log|·|_v kills torsion.

Formula (Bugeaud–Győry Lemma 3, (18)): 𝓞_S^×/𝓞_K^× is free of rank t and maps isomorphically onto the principal ideals generated by S-units, a subgroup of index i_S = h_S of the free group on 𝔭_1, …, 𝔭_t; choose a triangular basis (ε_i) = 𝔭_i^{a_ii}⋯𝔭_t^{a_it} with a_11⋯a_tt = i_S and complete it by a fundamental system of units; the determinant is block triangular.
The bounds follow from 1 ≤ h_S ≤ h_K, log N𝔭_i ≤ log P_S and, for the lower bound, from class-number-and-regulator-bounds (R_K ≥ 0.2) and N𝔭_i ≥ 2.
acceptance: For K = ℚ and S = {(p)}: R_S = log p.
For S = ∅: R_S = R_K.

nodes.title: A fundamental system of S-units of controlled height (Bugeaud–Győry Lemma 1)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K, s := #S + #(infinite places) ≥ 2, and δ_K > 0 with h(η) ≥ δ_K/d for every η ∈ K^× that is not a root of unity (one may take δ_K = d·m(d) from voutier-height-lower-bound). There is a fundamental system ε_1, …, ε_{s−1} of S-units with (i) ∏_i h(ε_i) ≤ c_4·R_S, (ii) h(ε_i) ≤ c_5·R_S for each i, and (iii) every entry of the inverse of the matrix (log|ε_i|_{v_j})_{i,j ≤ s−1} has absolute value at most c_6, where c_4 := ((s − 1)!)²/(2^{s−2}d^{s−1}), c_5 := c_4(δ_K/d)^{2−s} and c_6 := c_4 d^{s−1}δ_K^{−1}. (Here h is the absolute logarithmic height; Bugeaud–Győry write log h with h multiplicative.)
hypotheses: K a number field of degree d
S finite set of finite places, s ≥ 2
δ_K a lower bound as stated
proofSteps: Delete one coordinate from the S-logarithmic hyperplane and use the ℓ¹ gauge F in r = s−1 coordinates. The lattice covolume is R_S and the gauge ball has volume 2^r/r!. The successive-minimum witnesses and Minkowski upper bound give independent vectors v_i with ∏F(v_i) ≤ r! R_S.

To obtain the sharp basis factor, use the primitive flag Λ ∩ span(v₁,…,v_i) from GN.0/integral-rational-flag. In its rank-one quotient, write the image of v_i as m times a primitive generator. If |m| = 1, use ±v_i as the lift. If |m| ≥ 2, lift that generator as v_i/m plus a combination of the earlier v_j; subtract integer multiples of those v_j so each earlier coefficient has absolute value at most 1/2. This is still a primitive generator modulo the flag and has F-size at most iλ_i/2. These lifts form a lattice basis and satisfy F(ε_i) ≤ max(1,i/2)λ_i. This is a consumer proof of the sharp factor, rather than an assertion that the supplier’s weaker (i+1) factor preserves c₄.

For S-units the product formula gives F/(2d) ≤ h ≤ F/d. Multiplying the basis factors r!/2^{r−1} with the minima bound gives ∏h(ε_i) ≤ r!² R_S/(2^{r−1}d^r) = c₄R_S. Dividing by the height lower bounds for the other r−1 units gives (ii).

For (iii), expand each determinant minor. Its absolute value is bounded by the product of the ℓ¹ sizes of its rows; this follows directly by dropping the distinct-column restriction in the permutation sum. Divide by R_S, bound the product of all row sizes by d^r c₄R_S, and use F(ε_i) ≥ d h(ε_i) ≥ δ_K for the removed row. This gives c₆ and requires no unsupported Hadamard citation.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, S = {(p)} (s = 2): the system {p} has h(p) = log p = R_S, consistent with (i) since c_4 = 1/(d^{1}) = 1.
Without the lower bound δ_K, (ii) fails to follow from (i): the individual heights are controlled only through the others being ≥ δ_K/d.
For S = ∅ it gives a fundamental system of units with ∏ h(ε_i) ≤ c_4 R_K.

nodes.title: A representative of small height modulo m-th powers of S-units
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, S a finite set of nonzero primes, η_1, …, η_{s−1} a fundamental system of S-units and ℓ(η) := (log|η|_v)_{v ∈ S ∪ S_∞} ∈ ℝ^s. Put c(η) := (1/2)·Σ_j ‖ℓ(η_j)‖_1. For every nonzero S-integer α and every integer m ≥ 1 there is an S-unit ε with h(αε^m) ≤ (1/d)·log N_S(α) + m·c(η)/d. In addition, there is an S-unit ε with h(αε^m) ≤ d⁻¹log N_S(α) + m(39d^{d+2}R_K + (h_K/d)log Q_S), where Q_S = ∏_{𝔭∈S}N𝔭. This exact second form uses independent ordinary units and the Loher–Masser height-product bound, rather than the coarse full-S-unit basis estimate.
hypotheses: K a number field, S finite set of finite places
η a fundamental system of S-units
proofSteps: The vector u := ℓ(α) − (log N_S(α)/s)·(1, …, 1) lies in the hyperplane Σ_v x_v = 0, because the coordinates of ℓ(α) sum to log N_S(α) (s-norm); the S-unit lattice ℓ(𝓞_S^×) spans this hyperplane (s-unit-rank and s-logarithmic-map-kernel-and-lattice).

Write u = Σ_j x_j ℓ(η_j) and x_j = m·b_j + ϱ_j with b_j ∈ ℤ, |ϱ_j| ≤ m/2; with ε := ∏ η_j^{−b_j} one gets ℓ(αε^m) − (log N_S(α)/s)·(1, …, 1) = Σ_j ϱ_j ℓ(η_j), of ℓ¹-norm at most (m/2)·Σ_j‖ℓ(η_j)‖_1 (as in the proof of Bugeaud–Győry Lemma 2 for S = S_∞ and of DT.4/unit-lattice-covering-bound).
Since αε^m is an S-integer, h(αε^m) = (1/d)·Σ_{v∈S∪S_∞} max(0, log|αε^m|_v) ≤ (1/d)(log N_S(α) + m·c(η)) after summing the s coordinates.

For the exact BEG constant, first balance an algebraic integer using independent ordinary units from the successive minima. Their product of heights is at most r!R_K/d^r. Applying the independent-height-product lower bound to each omitted (r−1)-tuple bounds the largest height by 29e√(r−1)r!log d·R_K for r ≥ 2. The rounding estimate then has constant c₃ = 29e r! r√(r−1)log d; for r = 1 take c₃ = 1/d, and for r = 0 take c₃ = 0. Since r ≤ d−1, c₃ ≤ 39d^{d+2}.

For a general S-integer choose a generator π_𝔭 of 𝔭^{h_K} at each finite prime of S. Multiply α by m-th powers of these S-units to put its orders at those primes in [0,mh_K), leaving an algebraic integer α′ with log |N(α′)| ≤ log N_S(α) + mh_K log Q_S. Apply the ordinary-unit bound to α′. This proves the stated exact constant subject to the recorded quantitative height-product gap.
acceptance: For S = ∅ and m = 1 this is the balanced-unit-multiple bound of DT.4/balanced-unit-multiple, read as a height bound.
For K = ℚ, S = {(p)}, α = p^k·u (p ∤ u): one may take ε = p^{−⌊k/m⌉}, leaving h(αε^m) ≤ log|u| + (m/2)·log p.
The m-dependence is linear, which is what Lemma 4.2(ii) needs.

nodes.title: Every ideal class contains an ideal of small norm times a principal ideal
nodes.statement: Let L be a number field, T a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_L, and 𝔄 a nonzero fractional ideal of the T-integers 𝓞_T. There is ξ ∈ 𝔄 ∖ {0} such that (ξ) = 𝔅·𝔄 with 𝔅 an integral ideal of 𝓞_T of T-norm N_T(𝔅) ≤ |D_L|^{1/2}. In particular the classes of integral ideals of T-norm at most |D_L|^{1/2} generate the class group of 𝓞_T, and an element ξ can be found effectively.
hypotheses: L a number field, T finite
𝔄 a nonzero fractional ideal of 𝓞_T
proofSteps: Write 𝔄 = 𝔄*·𝓞_T with 𝔄* a fractional ideal of 𝓞_L supported outside T; scaling by a nonzero integer reduces to 𝔄* integral.

Minkowski's theorem in the form of Mathlib's exists_ne_zero_mem_ideal_of_norm_le_mul_sqrt_discr gives ξ ∈ 𝔄* ∖ {0} with |N_{L/ℚ}(ξ)| ≤ |D_L|^{1/2}·N(𝔄*) (the factor (4/π)^{r_2}d!/d^d ≤ 1 can be dropped).
Then (ξ) = 𝔅*·𝔄* with 𝔅* integral of norm ≤ |D_L|^{1/2}; passing to 𝓞_T can only decrease the norm, since the T-norm forgets the primes of T (s-norm).
acceptance: For L with class number 1 one may take 𝔅 = 𝓞_T and ξ a generator.
For L = ℚ(√−5), 𝔄 = (2, 1 + √−5): N(𝔄) = 2 and ξ = 2 gives (2) = 𝔄², so 𝔅 = 𝔄 with N(𝔅) = 2 ≤ √20.
The bound |D_L|^{1/2} is uniform in 𝔄.

nodes.title: Principal generators for powers of ideals and the finite set of class representatives
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with class number h and P a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K. (i) For every nonzero ideal 𝔞 of 𝓞_K, 𝔞^h is principal. (ii) Choose π_𝔭 ∈ 𝓞_K with (π_𝔭) = 𝔭^h for 𝔭 ∈ P and let Γ_P ⊆ K^× be the subgroup generated by 𝓞_K^× and the π_𝔭; it is finitely generated of rank rank(𝓞_K^×) + #P and has finite index h' ∣ h^{#P} in the P-units. (iii) For each nonzero ideal 𝔫 of 𝓞_K, the set R(𝔫) of principal ideals of the form 𝔞·∏_{𝔭∈P}𝔭^{r_𝔭} with 𝔞 ∣ 𝔫 supported outside P and 0 ≤ r_𝔭 < h is finite, and choosing one generator of each gives a finite set M_P(𝔫) such that every β ∈ 𝓞_K ∖ {0} with ord_𝔮(β) ≤ ord_𝔮(𝔫) for all 𝔮 ∉ P lies in μ·Γ_P for some μ ∈ M_P(𝔫).
hypotheses: K a number field with class number h
P a finite set of nonzero primes
proofSteps: (i): the class group is a finite group of order h (NumberField.classNumber, finiteness), so [𝔞]^h = 1 (pow_card_eq_one'), i.e. 𝔞^h is principal (ClassGroup.mk0_eq_one_iff).

(ii): Γ_P is generated by finitely many elements; an element of the P-units has (β) = ∏_{𝔭∈P}𝔭^{a_𝔭}, and β·∏π_𝔭^{−q_𝔭} with a_𝔭 = h q_𝔭 + r_𝔭 generates ∏𝔭^{r_𝔭}, a principal ideal from a finite list.

(iii): write (β) = 𝔞·∏_{𝔭∈P}𝔭^{a_𝔭} with 𝔞 ∣ 𝔫 supported outside P; reduce the exponents a_𝔭 modulo h using the π_𝔭; the remaining principal ideal belongs to R(𝔫), which is finite because 𝔫 has finitely many divisors (UniqueFactorizationMonoid.fintypeSubtypeDvd); two generators of one principal ideal differ by a unit.

nodes.title: Kernel and image of the S-logarithmic map
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, S a finite set of nonzero primes and ℓ : 𝓞_S^× → ℝ^{S ∪ S_∞}, ℓ(y) := (log|y|_v)_v with the normalised absolute values. Then (i) (integrality) an element y ∈ K^× with |y|_𝔭 ≤ 1 for all finite 𝔭 lies in 𝓞_K; (ii) (kernel) ℓ(y) = 0 if and only if y is a root of unity; (iii) (discreteness) for every B the set {y ∈ 𝓞_S^× : ‖ℓ(y)‖_∞ ≤ B} is finite, so ℓ(𝓞_S^×) is a lattice in the hyperplane Σ_v x_v = 0; (iv) consequently γ_1, …, γ_t ∈ 𝓞_S^× are multiplicatively independent modulo roots of unity if and only if ℓ(γ_1), …, ℓ(γ_t) are ℝ-linearly independent.
hypotheses: S a finite set of finite places
proofSteps: (i): an element of nonnegative order at every prime lies in every localisation, hence in 𝓞_K (Set.integer_eq with S = ∅ and IsDedekindDomain.integer_empty).

(ii): if ℓ(y) = 0 then |y|_𝔭 = 1 at all finite places, so y ∈ 𝓞_K by (i), and all conjugates have absolute value 1, so y is a root of unity (NumberField.Embeddings.pow_eq_one_of_norm_eq_one); conversely roots of unity have all absolute values 1.

(iii): ‖ℓ(y)‖_∞ ≤ B bounds the height h(y) ≤ (s/d)·B; Northcott's finiteness (NumberField.finite_setOfPred_logHeight₁_le) gives finitely many such y. A subgroup of ℝ^s with finitely many points in every ball is discrete, hence a lattice in its span, which lies in the hyperplane Σ_v x_v = 0 by the product formula.

(iv): a ℤ-relation among the ℓ(γ_j) is a multiplicative relation modulo the kernel, i.e. modulo roots of unity; a discrete subgroup's ℚ-independence equals ℝ-independence (Real.finrank_eq_int_finrank_of_discrete).

Mathlib’s finite_setOfPred_logHeight₁_le uses relative logarithmic height. DT.0/abs-mul-height-eq-rpow converts it to d times the absolute logarithmic height; the degree d is fixed here. The rank theorem then turns a discrete lattice in its real span into a full lattice in the (s−1)-dimensional hyperplane.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, S = {(2)}: ℓ(2^k·(−1)^e) = (k log 2, −k log 2), whose kernel is {±1}.
For K = ℚ(i), S = ∅: the kernel of ℓ on 𝓞_K^× = {±1, ±i} is the whole group.
This supplies the kernel and integrality steps used by DT.4/exponent-height-bound-for-finitely-generated-groups.

nodes.title: The S-unit theorem: 𝓞_S^× is finitely generated of rank r + #S
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field with unit rank r = r_1 + r_2 − 1 and S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K. Then the group 𝓞_S^× of S-units is finitely generated, its torsion subgroup is the group of roots of unity of K, and its rank is r + #S. Equivalently, with s := #S + r_1 + r_2, every fundamental system of S-units has s − 1 elements.
hypotheses: S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K
proofSteps: The valuation map 𝓞_S^× → ℤ^S, y ↦ (ord_𝔭 y)_{𝔭∈S} (Tau Ceti Set.unitValuation) has kernel 𝓞_K^× (Set.unitValuation_ker with Set.unitEmptyEquivUnits), which is finitely generated of rank r by Dirichlet's unit theorem (NumberField.Units.rank).
Its image contains h·ℤ^S: for 𝔭 ∈ S, 𝔭^h = (π_𝔭) is principal (principal-generators-of-class-group-powers) and π_𝔭 is an S-unit with valuation vector h·e_𝔭. Hence the image has rank #S.
Ranks add in the exact sequence 1 → 𝓞_K^× → 𝓞_S^× → image → 0 (the image is free), and finite generation is Set.unit_fg_of_units; the torsion lies in the kernel, i.e. in the roots of unity of 𝓞_K^×.
acceptance: For K = ℚ and S = {(2), (3)}: 𝓞_S^× = {±2^a3^b} has rank 2 = 0 + 2.
For K = ℚ(√2) and S = ∅: rank 1, generated with −1 by 1 + √2.
For K = ℚ(√−5), S = {(2, 1 + √−5)}: the S-units are ±2^k (rank 1), although the prime is not principal.

nodes.title: Gauss's lemma for content ideals over a Dedekind domain
nodes.statement: Let A be a Dedekind domain with fraction field F and, for f ∈ F[X] nonzero, let [f] be the fractional ideal of A generated by the coefficients of f. Then [fg] = [f]·[g] for all nonzero f, g ∈ F[X]. In particular, over a number field K containing all zeros α_1, …, α_n of f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n), [f] = [a_0]·∏_i [1, α_i]; and for every nonarchimedean place v the Gauss norm |f|_v := max_i |a_i|_v is multiplicative.
hypotheses: A a Dedekind domain, F = Frac A
proofSteps: Mathlib proves [fg] ⊆ [f][g] (Polynomial.contentIdeal_mul_le_mul_contentIdeal, stated for the integral content ideal; clear denominators by a common nonzero a ∈ A).

For the reverse inclusion localise at a nonzero prime 𝔭: A_𝔭 is a discrete valuation ring, where content ideals are generated by a coefficient of minimal valuation and Gauss's lemma (the product of primitive polynomials over a UFD is primitive, Polynomial.IsPrimitive.mul) gives equality of valuations. Equality of fractional ideals of a Dedekind domain can be checked locally at every prime.
The number-field statements follow from f = a_0∏(X − α_i) and [X − α_i] = [1, α_i]; the Gauss norm at v is N𝔭^{−ord_𝔭[f]}.
acceptance: For A = ℤ[√−5], f = 2X + (1 + √−5), g = 2X + (1 − √−5): fg = 4X² + 4X + 6, [f] = [g] = 𝔭 := (2, 1 + √−5) and [fg] = (2) = 𝔭², although neither content ideal is principal.
The inclusion [fg] ⊆ [f][g] alone (Mathlib's direction) does not give equality: the reverse inclusion is the Dedekind-specific part.

nodes.title: The logarithmic height of a polynomial and of a superelliptic equation
nodes.statement: For a number field K and f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ K[X], h(f) := (1/[K:ℚ])·Σ_{v ∈ M_K} log max(1, |a_0|_v, …, |a_n|_v), with the normalised absolute values of s-norm; equivalently h(f) is the absolute logarithmic height of the projective point (1 : a_0 : ⋯ : a_n), i.e. Mathlib's Height.logHeight of that tuple divided by [K:ℚ]. For b ∈ K, ĥ(b, f) := (1/[K:ℚ])·Σ_v log max(1, |b|_v, |a_0|_v, …, |a_n|_v). Both are independent of the number field containing the coefficients. For b ∈ ℤ and f ∈ ℤ[X]: ĥ(b, f) = log max(1, |b|, |a_0|, …, |a_n|), the convention of DT.4/baker-superelliptic-theorem.
proofSteps: Definition; independence of K is the extension invariance of the absolute height (sum over the places above v of the local degrees equals [L:K]).

h(X − 1/2) = log 2 (the 2-adic place contributes).

nodes.title: The height of a polynomial against the heights of its roots (BEG Lemma 3.6)
nodes.statement: For algebraic numbers α_1, …, α_n and f := (X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n): |h(f) − Σ_i h(α_i)| ≤ n·log 2. More generally, for a nonmonic polynomial f = a₀∏(X−α_i), a₀ ≠ 0, one has Σh(α_i) ≤ h(f) + n log 2. For evaluation, h(f(x)) ≤ h(f) + n h(x) + log(n+1).
proofSteps: Work in a number field containing the α_i. At a finite place the Gauss norm is multiplicative (content-ideal-gauss-lemma), so log max(1, |coefficients of f|_v) = Σ_i log max(1, |α_i|_v) exactly.

At an infinite place, with σ the corresponding embedding, the Mahler measure satisfies M(σf) = ∏_i max(1, |σα_i|) (Polynomial.mahlerMeasure_mul, mahlerMeasure_X_sub_C); each coefficient is at most C(n, k)·M ≤ 2^n·M (norm_coeff_le_choose_mul_mahlerMeasure) and M ≤ √(n + 1)·max|coefficient| ≤ 2^n·max|coefficient| (Landau, mahlerMeasure_le_sqrt_sum_sq_norm_coeff).
Summing over the places with weights (the multiplicity of a complex place counts twice, matched by s(v)) and dividing by [K:ℚ] gives the claim; the leading coefficient 1 makes max(1, …) harmless.

For a nonmonic polynomial use projective coefficient height first: the local Mahler measure of a₀∏(X−α_i) is |a₀| times the product of max(1,|α_i|). The product formula cancels the leading coefficient, and the projective coefficient height is bounded by the affine tuple height h(f). At an infinite place the coefficient maximum and Mahler measure differ by at most the factor 2^n; at finite places Gauss gives equality. Evaluation follows from the triangle inequality at infinity and the ultrametric inequality elsewhere, contributing log(n+1).
acceptance: For f = X − α the two sides agree exactly.
For f = (X − 1)^n: h(f) = log max_k C(n, k) ≤ n log 2 while Σ h(1) = 0, so the constant n·log 2 is needed up to lower-order terms.
For f = X² − 2 = (X − √2)(X + √2): h(f) = log 2 and Σ h(±√2) = log 2.

nodes.title: Size of the discriminant of a polynomial (BEG Lemma 3.7)
nodes.statement: Assume n ≥ 1. Let K be a number field and f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ K[X] of degree n with discriminant D(f) ≠ 0. Then (i) |D(f)|_v ≤ n^{(2n−1)s(v)}·max(|a_0|_v, …, |a_n|_v)^{2n−2} for every place v, where s(v) = 1, 2, 0 for real, complex and finite v; (ii) h(D(f)) ≤ (2n − 1)·log n + (2n − 2)·h(f).
hypotheses: f ∈ K[X] of degree n ≥ 1, D(f) ≠ 0
proofSteps: Finite v: D(f) (Mathlib's Polynomial.discr, a determinant in the coefficients) is a homogeneous polynomial of degree 2n − 2 in a_0, …, a_n with integer coefficients, so the ultrametric inequality gives (i) with s(v) = 0.

Infinite v: Bérczes–Evertse–Győry cite Lewis–Mahler (Acta Arith. 6 (1961), p. 335) for |D(f)| ≤ n^{2n−1}·max|a_i|^{2n−2}. A route through results in the libraries gives the slightly weaker |D(f)| ≤ n^n·M(f)^{2n−2} ≤ n^n(n + 1)^{n−1}·max|a_i|^{2n−2} ≤ e·n^{2n−1}·max|a_i|^{2n−2} (Mahler's discriminant inequality via Hadamard's inequality for the Vandermonde matrix, neither of which is in Mathlib at the pin, then Landau's bound mahlerMeasure_le_sqrt_sum_sq_norm_coeff); the extra factor e is absorbed in the constants that use this bound. The sharp form rests on gap 'Lewis–Mahler discriminant bound'.
(ii): multiply (i) over all places, take logarithms and divide by [K:ℚ]; Σ_v s(v) = [K:ℚ].
acceptance: For f = X² − 2: D(f) = 8 ≤ 2³·2² = 32 at the real place.
For f = aX² + bX + c: |b² − 4ac| ≤ 5·max(|a|, |b|, |c|)² ≤ 8·max(…)², consistent with n^{2n−1} = 8.
At a finite place the bound has no factor n^{…}, by the ultrametric inequality.

nodes.title: lcm(1, …, m) ≤ 4^m
nodes.statement: For every integer m ≥ 1, u(m) := lcm(1, 2, …, m) (Mathlib's Nat.lcmUpto) satisfies u(m) ≤ m^{π(m)} ≤ 4^m. A weaker bound u(m) ≤ 16^m·m^{√m} follows from results in Mathlib alone.
proofSteps: u(m) = ∏_{p ≤ m} p^{⌊log m/log p⌋} (Nat.factorization_lcmUpto) and p^{⌊log m/log p⌋} ≤ m, so u(m) ≤ m^{π(m)}.

Rosser–Schoenfeld's π(x) < 1.25506·x/log x for x > 1 (or Tijdeman's quoted π(k) ≤ 4k/(3 log k)) gives m^{π(m)} ≤ e^{1.256m} < 4^m. This explicit prime-counting bound is not planned in a roadmap of this or a lower upstream tier (gap 'Rosser–Schoenfeld prime-counting bound').
Mathlib's Chebyshev.pi_le_log4_mul_div gives π(m) ≤ 2 log 4·m/log m + √m and hence u(m) ≤ 16^m·m^{√m}, which can replace 4^m in Lemma 4.3 at the cost of larger numerical constants.

nodes.title: The relative discriminant divides the discriminant of a defining polynomial (BEG Lemma 3.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, L = K(α) and f ∈ K[X] a squarefree polynomial of degree m with f(α) = 0. Then, as fractional ideals of 𝓞_K, relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L) ⊇ [D(f)]·[f]^{−(2m−2)}; equivalently λ^{2m−2}·D(f) ∈ relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L) for every λ ∈ K with λf ∈ 𝓞_K[X]. (relDiscr is Tau Ceti's relative discriminant ideal, the relative norm of the different.)
hypotheses: K a number field, L = K(α)
f ∈ K[X] squarefree of degree m, f(α) = 0
proofSteps: Let g_1 be the irreducible factor of f with g_1(α) = 0, f = g_1g_2, n := deg g_1, k := deg g_2. Then D(f) = D(g_1)D(g_2)R(g_1, g_2)² (Tau Ceti Polynomial.Monic.discr_mul after normalising leading coefficients), and the determinant formulas give D(g_1) ∈ [g_1]^{2n−2}, D(g_2) ∈ [g_2]^{2k−2}, R(g_1, g_2) ∈ [g_1]^k[g_2]^n.

With [f] = [g_1][g_2] (content-ideal-gauss-lemma) this gives [D(f)]/[f]^{2m−2} ⊆ [D(g_1)]/[g_1]^{2n−2}, so it suffices to show D(h) ∈ relDiscr for every h = b_0X^n + ⋯ + b_n ∈ 𝓞_K[X], irreducible over K, with h(α) = 0.

Birch–Merriman: ω_i := b_0α^i + b_1α^{i−1} + ⋯ + b_i (0 ≤ i < n) are integral over 𝓞_K by induction on i (ω_iα is a root of a monic polynomial over 𝓞_L obtained from h(α) = 0), and the discriminant of the K-basis (1, ω_1, …, ω_{n−1}) of L equals b_0^{2n−2}·D_{L/K}(1, α, …, α^{n−1}) = D(h).
The discriminant of any K-basis of L consisting of integral elements lies in relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L) (request to Tau Ceti NumberFieldArithmetic, Layer 4).
acceptance: For K = ℚ, L = ℚ(i), f = X² + 1: relDiscr = (4) ⊇ (D(f)) = (−4).
For K = ℚ, L = ℚ(√5), f = X² − 5: relDiscr = (5) ⊇ (20), a proper inclusion (the index of ℤ[√5] is 2).
Scaling f by λ ∈ K^× does not change [D(f)][f]^{−(2m−2)}.

nodes.title: Exponents of the relative discriminant are bounded (BEG Lemma 3.2)
nodes.statement: Let L/K be an extension of number fields of degree n and u(n) := lcm(1, …, n). For every nonzero prime 𝔭 of 𝓞_K: ord_𝔭(relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L)) ≤ n·(1 + ord_𝔭(u(n))).
hypotheses: 𝔭 a nonzero prime of 𝓞_K
proofSteps: ord_𝔭(relDiscr) = Σ_{P∣𝔭} f(P|𝔭)·ord_P(𝔡_{L/K}) (Tau Ceti NumberFieldArithmetic, Layer 5.10). This exact dictionary is already implemented in current Tau Ceti as TauCeti.multiplicity_relDiscr; no duplicate target is planned. At the pinned baseline its verified NumberFieldArithmetic layer remains the supplier.
ord_P(𝔡_{L/K}) ≤ e(P|𝔭) − 1 + ord_P(e(P|𝔭)) (tame and wild bound, NumberFieldArithmetic Layer 6.4), and ord_P(e) = e(P|𝔭)·ord_𝔭(e) ≤ e(P|𝔭)·ord_𝔭(u(n)) because e(P|𝔭) ≤ n divides u(n).
Hence ord_𝔭(relDiscr) ≤ Σ_P f·e·(1 + ord_𝔭(u(n))) = n·(1 + ord_𝔭(u(n))) (Ideal.sum_ramification_inertia).
acceptance: For an unramified prime both sides are compatible with ord = 0.
For 𝔭 ∤ n! the bound reads ord_𝔭 ≤ n.

nodes.title: Discriminant of a compositum (BEG Lemma 3.3(ii))
nodes.statement: Let L_1, L_2 be finite extensions of a number field K inside a common field and M := L_1L_2. Then relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_M) ⊇ relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_{L_1})^{[M:L_1]}·relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_{L_2})^{[M:L_2]}. (Part (i) of BEG's Lemma 3.3, the tower formula relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_M) = relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L)^{[M:L]}·N_{L/K}(relDiscr(𝓞_L, 𝓞_M)), is Tau Ceti's relDiscr_tower.)
hypotheses: K ⊆ L_1, L_2 ⊆ M = L_1L_2 number fields
proofSteps: For a compositum M = L₁L₂ over K use Stark Lemma 6: the different of M/L₁ divides the extension to M of the different of L₂/K. Locally at a prime of L₂ choose an integral primitive element α whose minimal-polynomial derivative has the exact different order. The minimal polynomial over L₁ divides the one over K, so its derivative at α divides the old derivative; the different of M/L₁ divides that derivative. This is the local monogenic-choice/derivative bridge recorded below, not a trace-dual identity proved by a formal manipulation.

Take relative norms to K and use the discriminant tower formula. The norm of an extended L₂-ideal has the exponent [M:L₂]; the L₁ tower contributes d_{L₁/K}^{[M:L₁]}. This gives d_{M/K} ∣ d_{L₁/K}^{[M:L₁]}d_{L₂/K}^{[M:L₂]}. Iterate for more factors, using the corresponding compositum degrees.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, L_1 = ℚ(i), L_2 = ℚ(√2), M = ℚ(ζ_8): disc M = 2^8 divides 4²·8² = 2^{10}.
For L_2 = K the statement is trivial.
Linearly disjoint L_1, L_2 with coprime discriminants give equality.

nodes.title: Kummer extensions are unramified where the radicand is an m-th power up to a unit (BEG Lemma 3.4)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field, m ≥ 1, γ ∈ K^× and L := K(γ^{1/m}) for some m-th root. If 𝔭 is a nonzero prime of 𝓞_K with ord_𝔭(m) = 0 and ord_𝔭(γ) ≡ 0 (mod m), then 𝔭 does not divide relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L).
hypotheses: K a number field, m ≥ 1, γ ∈ K^×
proofSteps: Choose τ ∈ K with ord_𝔭(τ) = 1 and write γ = τ^{mt}ε with ord_𝔭(ε) = 0; then L = K(ε^{1/m}).
X^m − ε is squarefree (m ≠ 0 in K, ε ≠ 0) with discriminant ±m^m ε^{m−1}, so polynomial-discriminant-in-relative-discriminant gives relDiscr ⊇ [m^m ε^{m−1}]·[1, ε]^{−(2m−2)}.
The right side has 𝔭-order 0, and relDiscr is integral, so ord_𝔭(relDiscr) = 0.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, m = 2, γ = 3: L = ℚ(√3) is unramified at 5 (5 ∤ 2, ord_5(3) = 0) and ramified at 3.
For γ = 4·3 = 12 and 𝔭 = (2): ord_2(12) = 2 ≡ 0 mod 2 but 2 ∣ m, and ℚ(√12) = ℚ(√3) is ramified at 2: the hypothesis 𝔭 ∤ m matters.
For m = 1 the statement is trivial (L = K).

nodes.title: Discriminant of the field generated by roots of a polynomial (BEG Lemma 4.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and f ∈ K[X] of degree n with D(f) ≠ 0, f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over an extension, and L := K(α_1, …, α_k). Then |D_L| ≤ (n·e^{h(f)})^{2kn^k d}·|D_K|^{n^k}; for k = 1, |D_L| ≤ n^{(2n−1)d}·e^{(2n−2)d·h(f)}·|D_K|^{[L:K]}.
hypotheses: K a number field of degree d
f ∈ K[X] of degree n, D(f) ≠ 0
proofSteps: |D_L| = N_K(relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_L))·|D_K|^{[L:K]} (tower formula over ℤ: Tau Ceti relDiscr_tower and relDiscr_int_ringOfIntegers), and [L:K] ≤ n^k.
relative-discriminant-of-compositum applied to L = K(α_1)⋯K(α_k) and polynomial-discriminant-in-relative-discriminant give relDiscr(𝓞_K, 𝓞_{K(α_i)}) ⊇ [D(f)][f]^{−(2n−2)}.
By discriminant-size-bound at the infinite places and the definition of the norm at the finite ones, N_K([D(f)][f]^{−(2n−2)}) ≤ (n^{2n−1}e^{(2n−2)h(f)})^d.
Combine with [L : K(α_i)] ≤ (n − 1)⋯(n − k + 1).
acceptance: For k = 0 (L = K) the bound is |D_K| ≤ |D_K|.
The exponent of |D_K| is at most [L:K] ≤ n^k.

nodes.title: Discriminant of the auxiliary fields M (BEG Lemma 4.3)
nodes.statement: In the setting of superelliptic-power-decomposition (x − α_i = γ_iξ_i^m) let K have degree d and S consist of the infinite places and primes of norm product Q_S. (i) If m ≥ 3, M := K(α_1, α_2, (γ_1/γ_2)^{1/m}, ρ) with ρ a primitive m-th root of unity, then |D_M| ≤ 10^{m³n²d}·n^{4m²n³d}·|D_K|^{m²n²}·Q_S^{m²n²}·e^{4m²n³d·ĥ}. (ii) If m = 2 and M := K(α_1, α_2, α_3, √(γ_1/γ_2), √(γ_1/γ_3)), then |D_M| ≤ n^{40n⁴d}·Q_S^{8n³}·|D_K|^{4n³}·e^{25n⁴d·ĥ}.
proofSteps: (i): with L := K(α_1, α_2), M_1 := L((γ_1/γ_2)^{1/m}), M_2 := L(ρ): |D_M| = N_L(relDiscr(𝓞_L, 𝓞_M))·|D_L|^{[M:L]}, relDiscr(𝓞_L, 𝓞_{M_2}) ⊇ (m)^m (polynomial-discriminant-in-relative-discriminant for X^m − 1), and the compositum lemma gives relDiscr(𝓞_L, 𝓞_M) ⊇ m^{m²}·relDiscr(𝓞_L, 𝓞_{M_1})^m.

Primes P of L outside S not dividing m·a_0·b·D(f) have ord_P(γ_1/γ_2) ≡ 0 mod m (superelliptic-ideal-power-decomposition), so M_1/L is unramified there (kummer-extension-unramified-criterion); at the remaining primes relative-discriminant-exponent-bound gives exponent ≤ m(1 + ord_P(u(m))).

Bound the norm of the product of those primes by (Q_S·N_S(m a_0 b D(f)))^{n²} and u(m)^m ≤ 4^{m²} (lcm-of-first-integers-bound), N_S(D(f)) via discriminant-size-bound, and |D_L| by discriminant-of-root-field-bound with k = 2.
(ii) is the same computation with L := K(α_1, α_2, α_3), [L:K] ≤ n³ and two quadratic Kummer steps.
acceptance: The field M of (i) contains the splitting field of γ_1X^m − γ_2Y^m over K(α_1, α_2).
For m = 2 the field M of (ii) equals K(α_1, α_2, α_3, √(γ_1/γ_3), √(γ_2/γ_3)), the field used in BEG's proof of Theorem 2.2.
The dependence on Q_S enters only through the primes where M_1/L can ramify.

nodes.title: Effective finiteness of Thue equations over the S-integers
nodes.statement: Let M be a number field, T a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_M, β ∈ M^× and F ∈ M[X, Y] a binary form of degree n ≥ 3 with nonzero discriminant that splits into linear factors over M. Then {(x, y) ∈ 𝓞_T² : F(x, y) = β} is finite, and an explicitly computable finite set contains it: there are a finite set of pairs (a, b) ∈ (M^×)², computable from F, β, T, and a finitely generated group Γ ⊆ M^× with generators computable from M and T, such that every solution determines a solution (X, Y) ∈ Γ² of one of the unit equations aX + bY = 1, which lie in the explicit region of DT.4/gyory-equation-exponent-bound, and the solution is recovered from (X, Y) up to the at most n choices of an n-th root.
hypotheses: M a number field, T finite
F ∈ M[X, Y] of degree n ≥ 3, disc F ≠ 0, F a product of linear forms over M
proofSteps: Write F = l_1⋯l_n with pairwise non-proportional linear forms l_i = λ_iX + μ_iY (disc F ≠ 0) and choose δ ∈ 𝓞_M nonzero with δλ_i, δμ_i, δ^nβ ∈ 𝓞_M. For a solution, the T-integers δl_i(x, y) have product δ^nβ, so each divides δ^nβ in 𝓞_T.

After multiplying by an element of Γ := Γ_P (P := T; generated by 𝓞_M^× and generators of 𝔭^h, 𝔭 ∈ T) each δl_i(x, y) lies in 𝓞_M with ord_𝔮 ≤ ord_𝔮(δ^nβ) outside T, so DT.4/s-integral-divisor-representation (with its class-group step principal-generators-of-class-group-powers) gives δl_i(x, y) ∈ μ_iΓ with μ_i in an explicit finite set.

Three of the forms satisfy c_1l_1 + c_2l_2 + c_3l_3 = 0 with all c_i ≠ 0 (three pairwise non-proportional forms in two variables; DT.4/siegel-identity for l_i = X − θ_iY); dividing by c_3l_3 gives a(γ_1/γ_3) + b(γ_2/γ_3) = 1 with γ_i ∈ Γ and (a, b) from a finite set.

DT.4/gyory-effective-finiteness bounds the exponents of γ_1/γ_3, γ_2/γ_3 explicitly, so l_1(x, y)/l_3(x, y) takes finitely many computable values; l_3(x, y) ≠ 0 because F(x, y) ≠ 0. Each value fixes the ratio x : y, and F(x, y) = β then fixes (x, y) up to an n-th root of unity in M.

Coefficients of the linear factors need not be integral. Choose one nonzero denominator δ ∈ 𝓞_K so that all δl_i have S-integral coefficients, and replace the right-hand side by δ^{deg F}β. Apply the divisor-representative and unit-equation arguments to these integral values; undoing this fixed scaling only changes the computable bound.
acceptance: For M = ℚ, T = ∅ this is Thue's theorem (DT.4/thue-equation-effective-bound) with the content of F absorbed into δ.
For n = 2 the conclusion fails: x² − 2y² = 1 has infinitely many solutions in ℤ², which is why n ≥ 3 is required.
The splitting hypothesis is harmless: replace M by a splitting field of F and T by the primes above it.

nodes.title: Explicit bound for Thue equations over the S-integers (BEG Proposition 3.11)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d, S a finite set of places containing the infinite ones, of cardinality s, P_S := max N𝔭 and Q_S := ∏N𝔭 over the primes of S (both 1 if there are none), R_S the S-regulator, β ∈ K^×, and F = Σ_i a_iX^{n−i}Y^i ∈ K[X, Y] a binary form of degree n ≥ 3 with nonzero discriminant splitting into linear factors over K, with max_i h(a_i) ≤ A and h(β) ≤ B. Then every (x, y) ∈ 𝓞_S² with F(x, y) = β satisfies max(h(x), h(y)) ≤ c_1(s, d)·n⁶·P_S·R_S·(1 + log* R_S/log* P_S)·(R_K + (h_K/d)·log Q_S + ndA + B), with c_1(s, d) := s^{2s+4}·2^{7s+60}·d^{2s+d+2}.
hypotheses: K a number field of degree d, S ⊇ S_∞ finite, s = #S
F of degree n ≥ 3, disc F ≠ 0, split over K
β ≠ 0, heights bounded by A and B
proofSteps: Read Győry–Yu Corollary 3, p. 16, and its proof, pp. 38–39. First choose δ ∈ 𝓞_K clearing the coefficients with h(δ) ≤ ndA. Their Lemma 3 balances δ^nβ by an ordinary unit; the resulting integral equation has coefficient and right-hand-side height bounds controlled by A, B, R_K and log Q_S. Apply their Theorem 3 for the split triangularly connected binary form, and undo the scaling. This is the explicit refinement of the effective unit-equation reduction.

Theorem 3 is proved on pp. 34–37 by connected chains of linear factors: every triangle gives a two-term S-unit equation, the explicit S-unit bound controls ratios after a common unit scaling, and Cramer’s rule for two independent factors recovers the coordinates. Its exact constants inherit the Yu 2007 gap and the independent-height-product gap.

The BEG contract above is retained as the source statement. Its short comparison with Győry–Yu needs separate care: Győry–Yu impose A ≥ 1 and define c₃ = 0 in unit rank zero, so a comparison simply multiplying by c₃ is not a proof. Record the low-height floor and rank-zero constant absorption as a precise gap. Applying the original theorem with max(1,A) and max(1,c₃) gives a sound explicit alternative; deriving BEG’s smaller displayed contract still needs that absorption.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, S = {∞}: s = 1, P_S = Q_S = 1, R_S = 1, and the bound reads max(h(x), h(y)) ≤ 2^{67}·n⁶·(1 + nA + B)·2.
The bound is linear in A and B, as the S-unit method predicts.
The S-regulator itself is not monotone in S: over ℚ, R_∅ = 1 whereas R_{(2)} = log 2 < 1. No monotonicity claim about the whole bound is used.

nodes.title: Effective finiteness of systems of two Pell-type equations over the S-integers
nodes.statement: Let M be a number field, T a finite set of nonzero primes, and γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, β_12, β_13 ∈ M^× with β_12 ≠ β_13 and κ_2 := √(γ_1/γ_2), κ_3 := √(γ_1/γ_3) ∈ M. Then the system γ_1x_1² − γ_2x_2² = β_12, γ_1x_1² − γ_3x_3² = β_13 has finitely many solutions (x_1, x_2, x_3) ∈ 𝓞_T³, contained in an explicitly computable finite set.
hypotheses: M a number field, T finite
proofSteps: Put κ_23 := κ_3/κ_2 (a square root of γ_2/γ_3) and β_23 := β_13 − β_12 ≠ 0. The six linear forms u_± := κ_2x_1 ± x_2, v_± := κ_3x_1 ± x_3, w_± := κ_23x_2 ± x_3 satisfy u_+u_− = β_12/γ_2, v_+v_− = β_13/γ_3 and w_+w_− = β_23/γ_3, so all six are nonzero and, as in thue-equation-over-s-integers-effective, each lies in μ·Γ_T with μ from an explicit finite set (DT.4/s-integral-divisor-representation).

They satisfy the three-term identities κ_23u_+ − v_+ = w_− and κ_23u_− − v_− = −w_− (Evertse's Exercise 5.6 hint), so u_±/w_− and v_±/w_− solve two-term unit equations with coefficients from a finite set; DT.4/gyory-effective-finiteness gives finitely many values, explicitly.
Knowing the ratios u_+/w_−, u_−/w_− and the product u_+u_−, w_−² and hence w_− (up to sign), u_±, v_± are determined; then x_1 = (u_+ + u_−)/(2κ_2), x_2 = (u_+ − u_−)/2, x_3 = (v_+ − v_−)/2.

Coefficients of the linear factors need not be integral. Choose one nonzero denominator δ ∈ 𝓞_K so that all δl_i have S-integral coefficients, and replace the right-hand side by δ^{deg F}β. Apply the divisor-representative and unit-equation arguments to these integral values; undoing this fixed scaling only changes the computable bound.
acceptance: The system x_1² − 2x_2² = 1, x_1² − 3x_3² = 4 over ℤ needs √(1/2), √(1/3) ∈ M, so one works in M = ℚ(√2, √3) with T = ∅.
A single equation γ_1x_1² − γ_2x_2² = β_12 has infinitely many solutions in general (Pell); the second equation is what makes the set finite.
If β_12 = β_13 the identities degenerate (w_± are no longer nonzero), and the system can have infinitely many solutions (x_2 = ±x_3 when γ_2 = γ_3).

nodes.title: Explicit bound for systems of Pell equations over the S-integers (BEG Proposition 3.12)
nodes.statement: With K, S, s, P_S, Q_S, R_S, c_1(s, d) as in thue-equation-over-s-integers-explicit, let γ_1, γ_2, γ_3, β_12, β_13 ∈ K^× with β_12 ≠ β_13, √(γ_1/γ_2), √(γ_1/γ_3) ∈ K, h(γ_i) ≤ A and h(β_12), h(β_13) ≤ B. Then every solution (x_1, x_2, x_3) ∈ 𝓞_S³ of γ_1x_1² − γ_2x_2² = β_12, γ_1x_1² − γ_3x_3² = β_13 satisfies max_i h(x_i) ≤ c_1(s, d)·P_S·R_S·(1 + log* R_S/log* P_S)·(R_K + (h_K/d)·log Q_S + dA + B).
hypotheses: as in pell-system-over-s-integers-effective, with K in place of M
heights bounded by A and B
proofSteps: Put u_i = √(γ_i/γ₁)X_i. The six factors u₁±u₂, u₁±u₃, u₂±u₃ have rank three and a connected triangle graph: for example (u₁−u₂)+(u₂−u₃)=u₁−u₃; analogous triangles connect both signs. Multiply by a common denominator to make all factors integral and apply Győry–Yu Theorem 3 with nonzero product right-hand side β₁₂β₁₃(β₁₃−β₁₂), then undo the fixed scalar and square-root changes of coordinates.

Győry–Yu Theorem 3 and proof, pp. 15–16 and 34–37, give the explicit coordinate bound from the triangle S-unit estimates. The coefficient heights are bounded in terms of A and the right-hand-side height by 4B+log 2; recovering the original coordinates adds at most the square-root coefficient heights.

As for the Thue bound, the exact BEG constant is a verified source contract whose comparison still has the recorded A < 1 and rank-zero c₃ gap. The two explicit S-unit inputs are the independent-height-product bound and the exact finite-place Yu 2007 bound; neither is replaced by an unproved assertion about the Yu 1994 constant.
acceptance: The bound is the Thue bound without the factor n⁶ and with n replaced by 1 in nA.
β_12 ≠ β_13 is essential, as in the effective version.

nodes.title: The two factors of f(x) are almost coprime (BEG (4.9)–(4.10))
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. Put α := α_1, L := L_1, T := T_1, g := (X − α_2)⋯(X − α_n) ∈ L[X], and write [·] for fractional ideals of 𝓞_T. For every x ∈ 𝓞_S: (i) [x − α][1, α]^{−1} + [g(x)][g]^{−1} ⊇ [D(f)][f]^{−(2n−2)}; (ii) if f(x) = b·y^m with y ∈ 𝓞_S, then [b][f]^{−1}[y]^m = ([x − α][1, α]^{−1})·([g(x)][g]^{−1}). All four ideals [x − α][1, α]^{−1}, [g(x)][g]^{−1}, [α − α_i][1, α]^{−1}[1, α_i]^{−1} and [D(f)][f]^{−(2n−2)} are integral. The third ideal in the integrality list lives over the splitting field; the other three and the inclusions (i),(ii) are defined over L.
proofSteps: Over the splitting field: α − α_i = (x − α_i)·1 − (x − α)·1 gives [α − α_i] ⊆ [x − α_i][1, α] + [x − α][1, α_i]; dividing by [1, α][1, α_i], [x − α][1, α]^{−1} + [x − α_i][1, α_i]^{−1} ⊇ [α − α_i][1, α]^{−1}[1, α_i]^{−1}.

Multiplying over i = 2, …, n and using 𝔞 + ∏𝔟_i ⊇ ∏(𝔞 + 𝔟_i): the left side of (i) contains ∏_{i≥2}[α − α_i][1, α]^{−1}[1, α_i]^{−1}, which contains ∏_j∏_{i≠j}[α_j − α_i][1, α_j]^{−1}[1, α_i]^{−1} = [D(f)][f]^{−(2n−2)} by Gauss's lemma [f] = [a_0]∏[1, α_j] (content-ideal-gauss-lemma) and D(f) = ±a_0^{2n−2}∏_{i≠j}(α_i − α_j) (Tau Ceti Polynomial.discr_prod_X_sub_C).

The two normalized factors, their sum and product, and the discriminant/content ideal are defined over L. Their inclusion descends from the splitting field because extension of fractional ideals along the integral Dedekind extension is injective. Do not descend the individual pairwise root ideals, whose other root need not lie in L.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, S = ∅, f = X² − 1, α = 1: (i) says (x − 1) + (x + 1) ⊇ (4) = (D(f)), consistent with gcd(x − 1, x + 1) ∣ 2.
For f = 2X(X − 3) (Evertse's example (5.8)) and α = 0: (i) says (x) + (x − 3) ⊇ (9) = [D(f)][f]^{−2}, consistent with gcd(x, x − 3) ∣ 3.
Inclusion (i) is an ideal-theoretic gcd statement and does not need y.

nodes.title: x − α is an m-th power up to a bounded ideal (BEG Lemma 4.2(i))
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. Let x, y ∈ 𝓞_S with f(x) = b·y^m and y ≠ 0. Then for each i there are integral ideals 𝔆_i, 𝔄_i of 𝓞_{T_i} with [a_0(x − α_i)] = 𝔆_i𝔄_i^m and 𝔆_i ⊇ [a_0bD(f)]^{m−1}; in particular every prime of 𝓞_{T_i} dividing 𝔆_i divides a_0bD(f).
proofSteps: Take i = 1 (the others are symmetric). For a prime P of 𝓞_T not dividing a_0bD(f): P does not divide [f] (D(f) ∈ [f]^{2n−2}), so by superelliptic-factor-coprimality (i) it divides at most one of the two integral factors in (ii), whose product has P-order ≡ 0 (mod m); hence ord_P([x − α][1, α]^{−1}) ≡ 0 (mod m).
[a_0][1, α] is integral (a_0α is integral) and contains a_0, so it is prime to P; therefore ord_P(a_0(x − α)) ≡ 0 (mod m).
For the finitely many primes dividing a_0bD(f) write ord_P(a_0(x − α)) = m·q_P + r_P with 0 ≤ r_P < m and collect ∏P^{r_P} into 𝔆; then r_P ≤ (m − 1)·ord_P(a_0bD(f)) gives 𝔆 ⊇ [a_0bD(f)]^{m−1}.
acceptance: Evertse's example y³ = 2x(x − 3): 2x and x − 3 are cubes times divisors of powers of 6.
For f monic with D(f) = ±1 and b = 1 one gets 𝔆 = (1): x − α generates an m-th power of an ideal.
The bound on 𝔆 does not depend on x.

nodes.title: x − α = γξ^m with γ from an effectively computable finite set
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. There is a finite set Γ_{i,m} ⊂ L_i^×, computable from K, S, f, b and m, such that for every solution x, y ∈ 𝓞_S of f(x) = b·y^m with y ≠ 0 one has x − α_i = γ_iξ_i^m with γ_i ∈ Γ_{i,m} and ξ_i ∈ 𝓞_{T_i}.
proofSteps: By superelliptic-ideal-power-decomposition, [a_0(x − α)] = 𝔆𝔄^m with 𝔆 from the finite set of divisors of [a_0bD(f)]^{m−1}.

By minkowski-cofactor-for-ideals choose ξ_1 ∈ 𝔄 with (ξ_1) = 𝔅𝔄 and γ_1 with (γ_1) = 𝔇𝔆, where 𝔅, 𝔇 have T-norm at most |D_L|^{1/2}; there are finitely many such ideals, and generators can be fixed for the principal ones.
Then a_0(x − α) = (γ_1/γ_2)·ξ_1^m with (γ_2) = 𝔇𝔅^m, so γ_2 runs over generators of finitely many principal ideals, each determined up to a T-unit.

The T-units modulo m-th powers form a finite group (𝓞_T^× is finitely generated by s-unit-rank; Subgroup.finiteIndex_range_powMonoidHom_of_fg), so after moving m-th powers of T-units into ξ the factor γ := a_0^{−1}γ_1γ_2^{−1}·η runs over a finite computable set.
acceptance: For Evertse's example y³ = 2x(x − 3) (K = ℚ, S = ∅, α = 0, a_0 = 2): 2x = a·u³ with a ∈ {±2^k3^l : 0 ≤ k, l ≤ 2}, so x − 0 = (a/2)·u³ and Γ ⊆ {±2^{k−1}3^l : 0 ≤ k, l ≤ 2}.
If L has class number 1 and S = ∅, the ideals 𝔅, 𝔇 can be taken trivial, and Γ is a set of divisors of (a_0bD(f))^{m−1} times unit representatives.
The set Γ depends on m, which matters for variable exponents (superelliptic-variable-exponent-decomposition).

nodes.title: x − α = γξ^m with an explicit height bound for γ (BEG Lemma 4.2(ii))
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. For every solution x, y ∈ 𝓞_S of f(x) = b·y^m with y ≠ 0 there are γ_i ∈ L_i^× and ξ_i ∈ 𝓞_{T_i} with x − α_i = γ_iξ_i^m and h(γ_i) ≤ m·(n³d)^{nd}·e^{2nd·ĥ}·|D_K|^n·(80(dn)^{dn+2} + (1/d)·log Q_S), Q_S := ∏_{𝔭∈S}N𝔭.
proofSteps: As in superelliptic-power-decomposition, a_0(x − α) = (γ_1/γ_2)ξ_1^m with N_T(γ_1) ≤ |D_L|^{1/2}N_T(a_0bD(f))^{m−1} and N_T(γ_2) ≤ |D_L|^{(m+1)/2} (BEG (4.11)).

small-representative-modulo-s-unit-powers (BEG Lemma 3.8, constant c = 39d_L^{d_L+2}) gives T-units η_1, η_2 with h(γ_kη_k^m) ≤ d_L^{−1}log N_T(γ_k) + m(cR_L + (h_L/d_L)log Q_T); put γ := a_0^{−1}γ_1γ_2^{−1}(η_1η_2^{−1})^m and ξ := η_2η_1^{−1}ξ_1.

Bound the terms: d_L^{−1}log N_T(a_0bD(f)) ≤ h(a_0bD(f)) ≤ (2n − 1)log n + 2nĥ (s-norm, discriminant-size-bound); |D_L| ≤ n^{(2n−1)d}e^{(2n−2)dĥ}|D_K|^n (discriminant-of-root-field-bound, k = 1); max(h_L, R_L) ≤ 5|D_L|^{1/2}(log*|D_L|)^{nd−1} (class-number-and-regulator-bounds); Q_T ≤ Q_S^{[L:K]} (s-norm).
Inserting these into (4.12) gives the stated bound (BEG (4.13)–(4.15)).
acceptance: The bound is linear in m, which BEG's Theorem 2.1 needs.
For K = ℚ, S = ∅ it reads h(γ) ≤ m·n^{3n}·e^{2nĥ}·80·n^{n+2}.
Replacing class-number-and-regulator-bounds by computed h_L, R_L gives a valid bound for a given equation.

nodes.title: A superelliptic equation with m ≥ 3 reduces to Thue equations over S-integers
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. Let m ≥ 3 and let x, y ∈ 𝓞_S with f(x) = b·y^m, y ≠ 0, x − α_i = γ_iξ_i^m (i = 1, 2) as in superelliptic-power-decomposition. Let ρ be a primitive m-th root of unity, M := K(α_1, α_2, (γ_1/γ_2)^{1/m}, ρ) and T the primes of M above S. Then (ξ_1, ξ_2) ∈ 𝓞_T² solves the Thue equation γ_1X^m − γ_2Y^m = α_2 − α_1, whose binary form has nonzero discriminant and splits over M into the m pairwise non-proportional factors X − ρ^kθY times γ_1, with θ^m = γ_2/γ_1; conversely x = α_1 + γ_1ξ_1^m.
proofSteps: Subtract the two decompositions: γ_1ξ_1^m − γ_2ξ_2^m = (x − α_1) − (x − α_2) = α_2 − α_1, which is nonzero since D(f) ≠ 0 (BEG (4.23)).
The form γ_1X^m − γ_2Y^m has discriminant ±m^m(γ_1γ_2)^{m−1} ≠ 0 and factors as γ_1∏_k(X − ρ^kθY) over M.
The ξ_i are T_i-integers in L_i ⊆ M, hence T-integers of M.
acceptance: For Evertse's example (m = 3, f = 2X(X − 3), b = 1, α_1 = 0, α_2 = 3): γ_1ξ_1³ − γ_2ξ_2³ = 3 is a cubic Thue equation.
For m = 2 the binary form γ_1X² − γ_2Y² has only two factors, and Thue's theorem does not apply.
Each solution of the Thue equation gives at most m values of y with y^m = f(x)/b.

nodes.title: A hyperelliptic equation reduces to systems of two Pell equations
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. Let m = 2, n ≥ 3, and x, y ∈ 𝓞_S with f(x) = b·y², y ≠ 0, x − α_i = γ_iξ_i² (i = 1, 2, 3) as in superelliptic-power-decomposition. Let M := K(α_1, α_2, α_3, √(γ_1/γ_2), √(γ_1/γ_3)) (= K(α_1, α_2, α_3, √(γ_1/γ_3), √(γ_2/γ_3)), the field of BEG's proof of Theorem 2.2), [M:K] ≤ 4n³, and T the primes of M above S. Then (ξ_1, ξ_2, ξ_3) ∈ 𝓞_T³ solves γ_1ξ_1² − γ_2ξ_2² = α_2 − α_1, γ_1ξ_1² − γ_3ξ_3² = α_3 − α_1, a system as in pell-system-over-s-integers-effective with β_12 = α_2 − α_1 ≠ β_13 = α_3 − α_1.
proofSteps: Subtract the decompositions pairwise; α_2 ≠ α_3 gives β_12 ≠ β_13, and α_i distinct gives β_1j ≠ 0.
The two fields agree because each pair of square roots generates the third up to sign.
[K(α_1, α_2, α_3) : K] ≤ n(n − 1)(n − 2) ≤ n³ and two quadratic steps give [M:K] ≤ 4n³.
acceptance: Evertse's Exercise 5.7, y² = x(2x − 3)(4x − 5), leads to such a system.
With only two roots (n = 2) one gets a single Pell equation: y² = 2x² + 1 has the infinitely many integral solutions (2, 3), (12, 17), …, so n ≥ 3 is needed.
The field M is the same whichever two of the three square roots are adjoined.

nodes.title: Effective finiteness of superelliptic and hyperelliptic equations over S-integers
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. Assume n ≥ 3 if m = 2. Then the set of (x, y) ∈ 𝓞_S² with f(x) = b·y^m is finite and contained in an explicitly computable finite set; in particular an explicit bound for max(h(x), h(y)) can be computed from K, S, f, b and m.
proofSteps: y = 0 gives the at most n zeros of f in 𝓞_S.
For y ≠ 0, superelliptic-power-decomposition gives x − α_i = γ_iξ_i^m with γ_i from finite computable sets.
m ≥ 3: superelliptic-reduction-to-thue-equation and thue-equation-over-s-integers-effective give finitely many computable ξ_1, hence x = α_1 + γ_1ξ_1^m.
m = 2: hyperelliptic-reduction-to-pell-system and pell-system-over-s-integers-effective give finitely many ξ_1.
Each x gives at most m values of y.
acceptance: For K = ℚ, S = ∅ this is the effective content of DT.4/baker-superelliptic-theorem.
y² = x³ + 1 (m = 2, n = 3) has finitely many integral solutions, among them (−1, 0), (0, ±1), (2, ±3).
y² = 2x² + 1 (m = 2, n = 2) is excluded: it has infinitely many integral solutions (2, 3), (12, 17), …

nodes.title: Bérczes–Evertse–Győry bound for superelliptic equations (Theorem 2.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be a number field of degree d and discriminant D_K, S a finite set of nonzero primes of 𝓞_K (BEG's S also contains the infinite places; s := #S + #(infinite places)), 𝓞_S the S-integers, f = a_0X^n + ⋯ + a_n ∈ 𝓞_S[X] of degree n ≥ 2 with D(f) ≠ 0, b ∈ 𝓞_S ∖ {0}, m ≥ 2, ĥ := ĥ(b, f) (coefficient-height-of-polynomial), and f = a_0(X − α_1)⋯(X − α_n) over a splitting field; L_i := K(α_i) and T_i the primes of L_i above S. If m ≥ 3 and n ≥ 2, every solution x, y ∈ 𝓞_S of f(x) = b·y^m satisfies h(x), h(y) ≤ (6ns)^{14m³n³s}·|D_K|^{2m²n²}·Q_S^{3m²n²}·e^{8m²n³d·ĥ}, Q_S := ∏_{𝔭∈S}N𝔭. For K = ℚ, S = ∅, b ∈ ℤ and f ∈ ℤ[X] this is the explicit bound of DT.4/baker-superelliptic-theorem for n ≥ 3 (with N = deg f).
proofSteps: y = 0 is trivial. Otherwise superelliptic-power-decomposition-height-bound gives x − α_i = γ_iξ_i^m with h(γ_i) bounded, and superelliptic-reduction-to-thue-equation a Thue equation over the T-integers of M.

thue-equation-over-s-integers-explicit (BEG Proposition 3.11 over M, with #T ≤ m²n²s, [M:ℚ] ≤ m²n²d, P_T ≤ Q_T ≤ Q_S^{m²n²}) bounds h(ξ_1); the class number and regulator of M are bounded through discriminant-of-kummer-compositum-bound (C := the bound for |D_M|) and class-number-and-regulator-bounds, and R_T through s-regulator (BEG (4.24)–(4.28)).

Recover h(x) from the root-field variable with the nonmonic root-height estimate. Bound y by factorization, not an evaluation inequality missing log(n+1): m h(y) ≤ h(a₀)+h(b)+Σh(x−α_i) ≤ 3ĥ+n h(x)+2n log 2. The remaining constants are absorbed in the stated BEG bound as in §4, (4.28)–(4.30).
acceptance: For K = ℚ, S = ∅ (s = 1, d = 1, D_K = 1, Q_S = 1) the bound is (6n)^{14m³n³}·e^{8m²n³ĥ}, the bound recorded in DT.4/baker-superelliptic-theorem.
The bound is uniform in the solution and explicit in all data.
It does not apply to m = 2 (see beg-hyperelliptic-height-bound).
